Nkechi's first week at the school in Johannesburg, after moving from Lagos, was all watching.
At break, the girls already stood in circles, laughing at jokes she didn't understand. When she said “Good morning” in class, a boy copied her accent. She stopped saying much.
She ate her lunch on the steps, pretending to read, watching everyone. Nobody sat with her. She felt like a ghost, visible only when someone wanted to laugh.
On Thursday, a girl named Zanele sat down on the step beside her. “Is that jollof rice? My gran makes something like that. Can I taste?”
Nkechi held out the box. Her hand was shaking a little.

qa.q: Where did Nkechi eat her lunch?
qa.a: She ate her lunch on the steps.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel during her first week?
qa.a: She felt lonely and invisible, like a ghost, watching everyone and being noticed only when someone laughed.

qa.q: What small gesture helped, and why?
qa.a: Zanele sitting beside Nkechi and asking about her food was a kind, simple way of including her.

qa.q: How might Zanele have seen Nkechi before Thursday?
qa.a: She may have noticed the new girl alone on the steps and felt curious or sorry, and decided to reach out.

In the Chennai school canteen, every table had its group. Ayesha, new from Srinagar, stood with her tray.
The girls at the nearest table were chatting fast in Tamil. They glanced up, then back at each other. Ayesha didn't know one word. She walked to the end of the long table and sat alone.
For two weeks she noticed everything: who sat where, who laughed at whose jokes. Nobody noticed her. In class, when groups formed, she waited to be picked, and was picked last.
Then, on a Wednesday, Seema from her class waved from a crowded table. “Ayesha! Come, sit. I'll teach you one Tamil word a day. Today's is ‘saapadu’, food.”
Ayesha laughed for the first time in two weeks.

qa.q: What word did Seema teach Ayesha?
qa.a: She taught her "saapadu", food.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel during her first two weeks?
qa.a: She felt lonely and invisible, watching everything but not being noticed, and picked last.

qa.q: What made Seema's gesture so effective?
qa.a: It was warm and specific: a seat and a Tamil word a day, which gave Ayesha a way in.

qa.q: How might the girls at the nearest table have seen Ayesha?
qa.a: They probably didn't think much about her, just continuing their own chat without meaning to shut her out.

grounding: Shows a new child from another city finding groups already formed, feeling watchful and invisible until one kind gesture.

Monday: Chinmay's first day at the Guwahati school after moving from Pune. Everyone spoke Assamese at break. He stood near the water tank, watching football he wasn't asked to join.
Thursday: He had learned who the captain was, which boys were best friends, where the teachers stood. Nobody had learned his name. When the teacher said “Chinmay,” two boys said “Who?”
The next Wednesday: Ritu, who sat in front of him, turned around during art. “You draw well. Want to help us with the class wall?” Chinmay nodded too fast. That afternoon, he stood on a chair painting a rhino, while three classmates held the paint pots and asked him where Pune was.

qa.a: He stood near the water tank.

qa.a: He felt invisible and hurt, having learned everyone's names while nobody had learned his.

qa.a: Ritu inviting him to help with the class wall gave Chinmay a role and a reason to talk to others.

qa.q: How might the three classmates have seen Chinmay after the wall painting?
qa.a: They seemed curious and friendly, asking about Pune once they saw him as one of the team.

Yash, worried about the new school? Let your Lavanya paati tell you something.
When I was nine, my father's job moved us from Bhopal to Coimbatore. I spoke no Tamil. On my first day, the girls already had their hopscotch groups and tiffin circles. Every recess I stood near the water tap, washing my hands again and again. I watched everything, but I felt like a ghost. Nobody was cruel. That was the strange part. They just didn't see me.
On the eighth day, a girl called Kamala walked over with half a murukku and said something I didn't understand. Then she held up her fingers. "Onnu, rendu, moonu." One, two, three. She pulled me to the hopscotch squares.
I still remember how warm that murukku was.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya stand every recess?
qa.a: Near the water tap.

qa.q: How did young Lavanya feel during the first week?
qa.a: She felt invisible and lonely, "like a ghost", watching every group closely while nobody noticed her.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Kamala offered food and taught numbers through a game, which let Lavanya join in without needing Tamil first.

qa.q: Why might Kamala have walked over on the eighth day?
qa.a: Kamala may have noticed the new girl alone at the tap every day and felt kind or curious enough to try, even without a shared language.
